# Frequently asked questions

This FAQ answers Boundary's most common questions about networking requirements, Vault integration, identity provider support, and session monitoring.

## Q: What is the difference between HCP Boundary and self-managed Boundary?

HCP Boundary provides a managed control plane, while self-managed Boundary requires organizations to operate the controllers and database.
Both deployment models can use private workers in the networks that contain protected targets. The [Boundary edition documentation](/boundary/docs/what-is-boundary#which-edition-of-boundary-is-right-for-me)
provides additional details.

## Q: What are the networking requirements for Boundary?

Boundary workers require inbound access from clients. Workers do not necessarily need exposure to the public internet.
If the client is coming from a private network (eg a corporate network), the worker needs to allow connectivity from the private network.
If the client is coming from the public internet, the worker needs to allow connectivity from the public internet.
Boundary also supports multi-hop sessions, which chain workers across network boundaries and support environments with strict outbound-only policies.
The [worker networking requirements](https://developer.hashicorp.com/hcp/docs/boundary/self-managed-workers) provide additional details.

## Q: Which ports and network paths does Boundary require?

Clients reach the controller API listener on port `9200` by default, and workers reach controller cluster listeners on port `9201` by default.
Workers also need network paths to the targets they proxy, while clients need a path to the ingress worker. The [controller load-balancing documentation](/boundary/docs/architecture/load-balancing)
and [system requirements](/boundary/docs/architecture/system-requirements) describe the required listeners and network paths.

## Q: Can Boundary use multiple workers for high availability?

Yes. Organizations can deploy multiple ingress and egress workers with the same configuration in each network boundary to provide high availability.
Boundary's control plane selects and balances workers for sessions, so a load balancer should not distribute worker traffic. The [recommended architecture](/boundary/docs/architecture/recommended-architecture)
describes worker high-availability patterns.

## Q: Why does Boundary report that no workers are available?

Boundary reports this error when no worker can proxy the session to the target or when worker filters exclude all available workers.
Common causes include missing client-to-worker or worker-to-target connectivity, unavailable worker-to-controller connectivity, and worker filters that do not match.
The [worker error documentation](/boundary/docs/errors) and [worker filter documentation](/boundary/docs/workers/filters) describe these requirements.

## Q: Does Boundary require Vault? What is the integration story?

While Vault isn't a *required* secrets backend for Boundary sessions, the potential for Boundary | Vault integration is a core part of Boundary's overall
value proposition for identity-based access. There are three primary points of integration with Vault:
1. Vault can be used as a secrets backend for Boundary, offering single signon to end target systems via credential brokering. This was covered in Boundary's
[0.4 announcement](https://www.hashicorp.com/blog/announcing-hashicorp-boundary-0-4) and there are ample
[tutorials](/boundary/tutorials/credential-management/community-vault-cred-brokering-quickstart) of this scenario.
1. Boundary can use Vault as an OpenID Connect (OIDC) provider to enable sign-in with Vault's supported auth methods (even non-OIDC auth methods like Active Directory kerberos/LDAP).
This scenario is walked through in this [tutorial](/vault/tutorials/auth-methods/oidc-identity-provider).
1. Boundary can use Vault as the external key management system (KMS) that serves as Boundary's root of trust. More information on this use case can be found
in the [KMS configuration documentation](/boundary/docs/configuration/kms/transit).

## Q: Can Boundary use Vault to issue short-lived credentials?

Yes. Boundary can use a Vault credential store and credential library to retrieve credentials for a target.
Boundary can broker credentials to authorized users or inject them directly into sessions so users do not see them.
Vault can issue short-lived credentials through supported secrets engines. Boundary also
supports generic secrets from Vault. The [Vault integration documentation](/boundary/docs/vault) provides additional details.

## Q: How does Boundary connect to a private Vault instance?

Boundary can route Vault requests through a worker in the same network as a private Vault instance.
A worker filter identifies the workers that can reach Vault, while the Vault credential store uses those workers to relay requests to the controllers.
The [Vault credential store documentation](/boundary/docs/credentials/static-cred-vault) and [worker filter documentation](/boundary/docs/workers/filters)
provide additional details.

## Q: What is the difference between credential brokering and credential injection?

Credential brokering returns credentials to an authorized user when the user connects to a target.
Credential injection places credentials directly into an SSH or RDP session without exposing them to the user.
Boundary supports both workflows through static and Vault credential stores. The [credential brokering documentation](/boundary/docs/credentials/configure-credential-brokering)
and [credential injection documentation](/boundary/docs/credentials/configure-credential-injection) describe the differences.

## Q: What identity providers does Boundary support?

Boundary supports password, LDAP, and [OpenID Connect (OIDC) authentication](/boundary/tutorials/identity-management/oidc-auth0).
OIDC authentication supports many identity providers (IdPs), including Okta, Microsoft Entra ID (formerly Azure AD), Auth0,
and other compatible providers. Boundary also supports LDAP authentication natively. Users can also log in using an OIDC bridge identity provider, such as
[Vault's OIDC bridge](https://developer.hashicorp.com/vault/docs/concepts/oidc-provider) or [Dex](https://dexidp.io).
Refer to the [Boundary authentication documentation](/boundary/docs/authentication) and [auth method documentation](/boundary/docs/domain-model/auth-methods)
for more information.

## Q: Can identity-provider groups be used to assign access in Boundary?

Yes. Boundary can evaluate OIDC claims or LDAP group membership and use that information to place authenticated accounts into managed groups.
Administrators can assign managed groups as principals in Boundary roles. This enables identity-driven authorization without requiring administrators to assign every user individually.
The identity provider supplies identity or group information, while Boundary roles continue to define the permissions granted to those users.

## Q: Does Boundary support multi-factor authentication (MFA)?

Boundary supports MFA through an OpenID Connect (OIDC) identity provider that enforces it, such as Microsoft Entra ID, Okta, Auth0,
and other providers. The identity provider performs the MFA challenge, and Boundary receives the authenticated identity.
Boundary evaluates permission claims from an IdP-managed identity to determine managed-group membership. Managed groups support
dynamic role assignments based on identity attributes. See Boundary's [managed groups capabilities](/boundary/tutorials/identity-management/oidc-idp-groups).

## Q: Does Boundary automate the discovery and configuration of new targets (e.g. servers)? What happens if a host IP address changes?

Yes, this is one of the core competencies of Boundary. Boundary can discover new targets in two primary ways
1. Boundary's [Terraform provider](https://registry.terraform.io/providers/hashicorp/boundary/latest/docs) supports discovery of targets provisioned by Terraform
2. Boundary's [dynamic host catalog](/boundary/docs/hosts#dynamic-host-catalogs)
agentlessly queries infrastructure providers to automate the onboarding and configuration of hosts

All of these methods will automate the discovery and configuration of targets when their ip addresses change. Of course, static hosts can still be manually added via Boundary admin UI and CLI.

For more information on dynamic host catalogs, refer to:

- [AWS dynamic host catalogs](/boundary/docs/hosts/aws)
- [Azure dynamic host catalogs](/boundary/docs/hosts/azure)
- [GCP dynamic host catalogs](/boundary/docs/hosts/gcp)

## Q: Session management capabilities - Does Boundary support live session monitoring and termination?

**Session Logging/Monitoring:** Supported. Boundary creates a session log of all sessions created between identities and targets that have been onboarded to
Boundary. You can learn how to monitor these sessions in the [Manage sessions tutorial](/boundary/tutorials/community-administration/community-manage-sessions).
Boundary supports [audit logs](/boundary/tutorials/self-managed-deployment/event-logging) and [audit log streaming](https://developer.hashicorp.com/hcp/docs/boundary/audit-logging)
for HCP Boundary. Audit logs for both distributions can be exported to SIEM or BI tools.

**Session Termination:** Supported. Session termination for Boundary administrators is a supported capability, as demonstrated in this
[Manage sessions tutorial](/boundary/tutorials/community-administration/community-manage-sessions).

## Q: Can organizations define retention policies for session recordings?

Yes. Boundary storage policies define minimum retention periods and automatic deletion periods for session recordings.
Policies can apply at different scopes. When multiple policies apply, Boundary evaluates the effective retention and deletion requirements
according to its resultant set of policy rules. Retention takes precedence over deletion, the longest applicable retention period wins,
and the shortest applicable deletion period wins after Boundary satisfies the retention requirements. Refer to the [storage policy documentation](/boundary/docs/session-recording/compliance/configure-storage-policy)
for more information.

## Q: What happens to session recordings when a storage policy changes?

Updated storage policies apply to new session recordings in associated scopes. Existing recordings retain their previous policies unless an administrator
applies the updated policy retroactively. The [storage policy update documentation](/boundary/docs/session-recording/compliance/update-storage-policy)
describes how policy changes affect existing recordings.

## Q: As an AWS user, can IAM roles be used to configure Boundary's dynamic host catalog?

Yes. Boundary supports IAM role authentication for AWS dynamic host catalogs through `AssumeRole`.
The role must be assigned to a self-managed worker in the AWS account, and the host catalog must use a worker filter
that matches the worker. Refer to the
[AWS dynamic host catalog documentation](/boundary/docs/hosts/aws) for more information.
